projects.title: So Long and Thanks for All the Fish

pages.text:
So Long, and Thanks for All the Fish began with an accidental encounter.

  During the summer after my graduation, I walked into an aquarium.

  There, I found myself observing the lives existing behind glass: slowly rising bubbles, artificial lights changing the color of water, reflections appearing and disappearing on the surface, and fish moving through this small constructed world.

  At that period of my life, I was experiencing a moment of suspension. The future was uncertain, some expectations remained unanswered, and some distances between people could not be crossed.

  Initially, I only wanted to photograph what I saw. However, I gradually realized that I was recording a state of observation — a way of existing during uncertainty.

  While making this work, I remembered Douglas Adams’ novel So Long, and Thanks for All the Fish. The absurd yet gentle feeling of farewell within the title resonated with my experience in front of the aquarium.

The fish are not symbols of something else.

  They simply exist within their own world, moving through the water, appearing and disappearing from view.

  Perhaps that was what kept me looking.

  This book is not a story about fish.

  It is a record of observation, suspension, and the small moments that quietly offer comfort.

  So long, and thanks for all the fish.

projects.title: My life is a story of the self-realization of the unconscious

images.text: [A sentence about this image, in your own words.]

pages.text:
My life is a story of the self-realization of the unconscious.

For some reason, I thought of this quote by C.G. Jung.

I do not know why certain images feel familiar.

A tree, a shadow, a grave, the remains of ancient life. They belong to different places and different times, yet something draws them together.

I try to approach a feeling that resists explanation, as if these scenes could remember something that I cannot.
